guide.title: Period 3 (1754–1800): review guide
guide.intro: Britain's victory in the Seven Years' War set off a chain of new taxes, colonial protests, and ideas about rights that led to independence. Americans then experimented with governments, wrote a Constitution, and argued over what kind of republic they had created.

sections.title: From the Seven Years' War to independence
body: The Seven Years' War (French and Indian War, 1754–1763) removed France from North America but left Britain deeply in debt. Britain's Proclamation of 1763 limited settlement west of the Appalachians, and new taxes such as the Stamp Act (1765) and Townshend duties provoked protests over “taxation without representation.”

Enlightenment ideas about natural rights and Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776) helped turn protest into a call for independence. With help from France after the victory at Saratoga (1777), the Continental Army won independence, confirmed by the Treaty of Paris (1783).
points: Causation: war debt → taxes → protest → independence.
Colonists objected to Parliament taxing them without colonial representation.

sections.title: The Articles, the Constitution, and the new republic
body: The Articles of Confederation created a weak central government with no power to tax or regulate trade, though it passed the Northwest Ordinance (1787). Shays' Rebellion (1786–1787) convinced many leaders that a stronger government was needed. The Constitution (1787) created a federal system with separated powers and checks and balances; it contained compromises over representation and slavery.

Federalists, such as Madison in The Federalist No. 10, argued that a large republic would control factions; Anti-Federalists feared distant power and demanded a bill of rights, added in 1791. Under Washington and Adams, debates over Hamilton's financial plan, foreign policy, and the Alien and Sedition Acts produced the first political parties.
points: Continuity and change: fears of concentrated power persisted from the Revolution into the 1790s.
The Bill of Rights answered Anti-Federalist concerns.

sections.title: Revolutionary ideals, identity, and movement
body: Revolutionary ideals raised questions about who was included in “all men are created equal.” Some northern states began gradual emancipation; women's roles as educators of virtuous citizens were stressed (“republican motherhood”); and writers such as the formerly enslaved poet Phillis Wheatley challenged ideas about race.
After independence, settlers pushed west across the Appalachians, leading to conflict with American Indian nations, and a distinct American culture and identity began to form.
points: Ideals of liberty created contradictions with slavery.
Western migration increased conflict with American Indians.

example.prompt: Explain one way the Seven Years' War led to colonial resistance.
example.solution: The war left Britain with large debts, so Parliament imposed new taxes on the colonies, such as the Stamp Act of 1765. Colonists protested that Parliament, in which they had no representatives, had no right to tax them.

misconceptions: “Colonists wanted independence as soon as taxes began.”
Many first sought their rights as British subjects; independence came after years of conflict.
“The Bill of Rights was part of the original Constitution.”
It was added in 1791 after ratification debates.
Some northern states began gradual emancipation; slavery continued and grew in the South.

passages.title: Source A: James Madison, The Federalist No. 10, 1787
text: “From this view of the subject, it may be concluded, that a pure Democracy, by which I mean a Society consisting of a small number of citizens, who assemble and administer the Government in person, can admit of no cure for the mischiefs of faction. . . . A Republic, by which I mean a Government in which the scheme of representation takes place, opens a different prospect, and promises the cure for which we are seeking. . . . The two great points of difference, between a Democracy and a Republic, are, first, the delegation of the Government, in the latter, to a small number of citizens elected by the rest: Secondly, the greater number of citizens, and greater sphere of country, over which the latter may be extended.”
passages.attribution: James Madison, The Federalist No. 10, an essay published in New York newspapers urging ratification of the Constitution, 1787. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 7.4.

StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/7-4-the-constitutional-convention-and-federal-constitution); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: Phillis Wheatley, “On Being Brought from Africa to America,” 1773
text: “Twas mercy brought me from my Pagan land, / Taught my benighted soul to understand / That there’s a God, that there’s a Saviour too: / Once I redemption neither sought nor knew. / Some view our sable race with scornful eye, / “Their colour is a diabolic dye.” / Remember, Christians, Negroes, black as Cain, / May be refin’d, and join th’ angelic train.”
passages.attribution: Phillis Wheatley, an enslaved poet in Boston, from Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral, 1773. (Line breaks are shown with slashes.) Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 7.2.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/7-2-how-much-revolutionary-change); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of the road to revolution
text: “The war that drove France from North America in 1763 also loosened the ties that held Britain's colonies to the empire. Victory left Britain with a staggering debt, and Parliament reasonably expected the colonists, who had been defended by British troops, to help pay it. But the colonists had grown used to governing themselves through their own assemblies, and new taxes passed in London seemed to threaten that tradition. What began as a dispute over money became a dispute over who had the right to govern.”

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of the Articles of Confederation
text: “The Articles of Confederation reflected the lessons of the Revolution: Americans who had just thrown off a distant, powerful government were in no hurry to create another. Congress could not tax, could not regulate trade between the states, and could not easily raise an army. Yet the Confederation was not a complete failure. Its Northwest Ordinance established an orderly process for creating new states, and it banned slavery in the territory north of the Ohio River.”

questions.prompt: Madison's main purpose in the excerpt is to argue that
choices: the states should remain fully independent
a pure democracy is the best form of government
a large republic with elected representatives can control the dangers of faction
the United States should have a king
questions.explanation: He says a republic, through representation and a larger territory, “promises the cure” for faction.
choiceExplanations: He supports the Constitution's stronger union.
He argues that pure democracy cannot cure faction.
He argues for a republic, not monarchy.

declare independence from Britain
oppose the Bill of Rights
elect Thomas Jefferson president

choiceExplanations: Independence had been declared in 1776.
The essays didn't argue against a bill of rights in this way.

questions.prompt: Which group most strongly disagreed with Madison's claim that a large republic would protect liberty?
choices: Anti-Federalists, who feared that a distant central government would threaten the rights of the people
French allies of the United States
Federalists who wrote the Constitution
Loyalists who supported the king
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists argued that republics worked best in small areas and that a strong national government could become tyrannical.
choiceExplanations: The French weren't part of the ratification debate.
Federalists agreed with Madison.
Loyalists were no longer a force in this debate.

choices: The Proclamation of 1763
The addition of the Bill of Rights in 1791
Shays' Rebellion
The Northwest Ordinance
questions.explanation: Promising amendments that protected individual rights helped win over Anti-Federalists.
choiceExplanations: The Proclamation was a British policy from 1763.
Shays' Rebellion came before the Constitution and pushed for a stronger government.
The Ordinance predated ratification and concerned western lands.

choices: argue for independence from Britain
describe life in Africa
challenge the belief that Africans were inferior
praise the slave trade
questions.explanation: She reminds “Christians” that Black people “may be refin’d” and join the “angelic train,” rejecting the “scornful eye.”
choiceExplanations: The poem doesn't discuss independence.
Africa is mentioned only as her origin.
Her point is about equality before God, not praise of the trade.

military service in the Revolution

questions.prompt: The publication of Wheatley's poems in 1773 is best understood in the context of
choices: the Great Awakening's rejection of all written texts
laws requiring enslaved people to be educated
the end of slavery in all the colonies
growing debates about liberty and slavery as tensions with Britain increased
questions.explanation: As colonists spoke of liberty, writers like Wheatley highlighted the contradiction with slavery.
choiceExplanations: Revivalists didn't reject texts.
No such laws existed; many colonies discouraged teaching enslaved people.
Slavery continued in every colony in 1773.

The Alien and Sedition Acts

questions.explanation: Revolutionary ideals helped lead northern states to begin ending slavery.
choiceExplanations: That was a British policy on western settlement.
Those acts targeted immigrants and political critics.
That compromise protected slaveholders' political power.

To fund French settlements
To pay for the Revolutionary War

France had lost its North American colonies.
The Revolution came later.

The Bill of Rights
The Northwest Ordinance
questions.explanation: The Stamp Act taxed printed materials and provoked widespread protest.
choiceExplanations: That was a colonial agreement from 1620.
That was an American document from 1791.
That was passed by the American Congress in 1787.

questions.prompt: The passage's statement that colonists “had grown used to governing themselves through their own assemblies” best supports which claim?
choices: Long experience of self-government had given colonists a political identity distinct from Britain's
Parliament had always closely controlled colonial assemblies
Colonists wanted France to govern North America
Colonists had no tradition of representative government
questions.explanation: Decades of governing through their own assemblies shaped how colonists saw their rights, so taxes from London felt like a threat to that tradition.
choiceExplanations: This describes salutary neglect in reverse; Parliament had loosely enforced its rules.
France had just been driven from North America.
The passage says the opposite.
